core: Definition of absorption: digested nutrients pass from the digestive tract into the body (attributed to NIDDK and OpenStax)
Small intestine as the main site of absorption and why (surface area)
Villi and microvilli increase the absorbing surface area
What gets absorbed: nutrients, water, and some minerals
Different routes in: simple sugars and amino acids to the blood directly; fats via the lymph system first
Delivery: absorbed nutrients enter the bloodstream and are carried to the body; liver as processing hub
What is NOT absorbed: undigested material passes through and leaves as waste
supporting: Absorption is step three of the pipeline ingestion, digestion, absorption, metabolism
Large intestine recovers additional water and electrolytes from waste material before stool forms
The body breaks nutrients into absorbable parts (proteins to amino acids, fats to fatty acids and glycerol, carbohydrates to simple sugars)
Metabolism is the step that follows absorption (sibling topic, referenced only)
Fiber moves through the digestive system undigested (sibling topic, referenced only)
outOfScope: Metabolic pathways and energy use (own topic: metabolism)
Cellular and molecular mechanisms of transport (biology subject owns cellular depth)
Fiber types and health effects (own topic: fiber)

claims.claim: Absorption is the process by which digested nutrients pass from the digestive tract into the body; the digestive system breaks nutrients into parts small enough for the body to absorb and use for energy, growth, and cell repair.

Absorption is step three of the food pipeline: ingestion, digestion, absorption, and metabolism; absorption is when cells take in the broken-down substances, and metabolism is when those substances are converted to energy.
The small intestine absorbs most of the nutrients in food, and its walls absorb water and digested nutrients into the bloodstream.
The surface area of the small intestine is increased by villi and microvilli that cover its walls, which promotes increased absorption.
Simple sugars, amino acids, glycerol, and some vitamins and salts are carried from the intestine by the blood to the liver; the lymph system absorbs fatty acids and vitamins.
The circulatory system passes absorbed nutrients on to other parts of the body to store or use, with the liver storing, processing, and delivering nutrients.
The large intestine absorbs water from waste material and changes the waste from liquid into stool; OpenStax notes water and electrolytes are absorbed from the feces in the large intestine.
Not everything eaten is absorbed: undigested parts of food, fluid, and older cells from the gut lining continue through the tract and leave the body as stool.
Fiber is made of plant substances such as cellulose and moves through the digestive system in an undigested form.
The body breaks nutrients into parts small enough to absorb: proteins into amino acids, fats into fatty acids and glycerol, and carbohydrates into simple sugars.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Where water and minerals are absorbed
positions: NIDDK emphasizes the small intestine absorbing water and digested nutrients into the bloodstream and the large intestine absorbing water from waste material
OpenStax notes water and electrolytes are absorbed from the feces in the large intestine, while also describing extensive capillary networks in the small intestine
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The sources agree on the overall picture, which the lesson states: most nutrients and most water are absorbed in the small intestine, and the large intestine recovers additional water and electrolytes from waste material before stool forms.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether fats enter the blood directly
positions: NIDDK states the lymph system absorbs fatty acids and vitamins, implying a two-stage route for fats
Popular summaries sometimes collapse the route and say all nutrients enter the bloodstream
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the source-supported two-route picture at literacy level: simple sugars and amino acids enter the blood directly, while fat breakdown products go through the lymph system before reaching the bloodstream.

sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Tier A government source. Supports: nutrients broken into parts small enough to absorb; small intestine as the site that absorbs most nutrients and absorbs water and digested nutrients into the bloodstream; circulatory system passing nutrients on to the body to store or use; liver as storage/processing hub; blood carrying simple sugars, amino acids, glycerol, and some vitamins and salts; lymph system absorbing fatty acids and vitamins; large intestine absorbing water and changing waste into stool; waste consisting of undigested parts of food, fluid, and older cells. Facts synthesized; only short phrases quoted with attribution.
